newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela reform program bursts into life.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela reform program bursts into life.

text.p: Venezuela's economic reform program, once considered by many analysts as more wish list than concrete program, has burst into life in recent weeks forcing even the staunchest doubters to reassess the country's progress.
But even with the sudden spate of reforms and initiatives, tough tests lie ahead and the government's commitment to real change is still questioned, analysts said.
"The reforms are very welcome. But sometimes I cannot tell when looking at Venezuela whether the glass is half full or half empty," one New York-based investment banker said.

Fast on the heels of a highly successful auction round of state oil fields to foreign multinationals and a breakthrough Labor Law reform, officials presented Congress Thursday with a model contract to privatize the aluminum industry.
Another reform, to open up the domestic gasoline retailing sector to competition from private companies, was due to be handed over to Congress Thursday afternoon.
"It certainly looks like we're getting back on the right track," one local analyst said.

The Caracas Stock Market has soared on the news, with prices bursting through successive technical ceilings. After a sluggish start, the .IBC general index has risen over 30 percent in real terms this year.

When Venezuela's President Rafael Caldera launched an IMF-backed reform program in April last year, murmurs of skepticism drowned the sighs of relief that Venezuela had finally embraced free market reforms.
"Very few people, including myself, thought this would happen," the Caracas-based analyst said.
Fourteen months later many doubts remain.

The most-needed reform -- a massive reduction in the bulging state bureaucracy which employs on out of every 20 Venezuelans -- has barely got off the ground, although the recent reform to severance payments system should give the government elbow room to start lay-offs next year.

And the continued success of the oil sector, which under the enlightened management of officials at state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA) goes from strength-to-strength, means that the urgency for reform is less acute than in other Latin American countries.

Even if the $3 billion steel and aluminum company privatizations go through this year as planned, that will be more than a year behind schedule and the recent Labor Law reform still has to be complemented by legislation to reform the social security system and create private pension funds.
Caracas-based political strategist Michael Rowan compared the reform process in Venezuela to pulling teeth without anesthesia.

"No doubt Venezuela is trying to change...Yet each achievement is sapped of its sweet success, when finally it comes, because of the time-consuming, debilitating political process needed to effect it," Rowan wrote in a newspaper column published Thursday.
Some analysts fear that Caldera still harbors grave doubts about the benefits of free market policies.
"My main concern is I don't see who or what is driving the reforms," the New York banker said.
But the reforms have come, albeit slowly, in an atmosphere of almost unprecedented political consensus.

And as leader of a political movement which will probably expire at the end of his presidency, 81-year-old Caldera has less to gain from holding up reforms to play politics as Venezuela approaches December 1998 elections.
"This government has a great advantage over previous governments -- they're not playing the game of re-election," the Caracas-based analyst said.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
